“All sentient beings, from beginningless time, have all manner of inversions, like a confused person who mistakes the four directions for other directions, deludedly taking the four great elements as the mark of their own body and the shadowy traces of the six sense objects as the mark of their own mind. It is like a diseased eye seeing flowers in the sky and a second moon. Good man! The sky truly has no flowers; the diseased one deludedly clings to them. Because of deluded clinging, he is not only confused about the self-nature of this emptiness, but also deluded about where those real flowers arise. From this delusion there is falsely the turning around in birth and death, and so it is called ignorance.”

Once the mark of self is established, the marks of person, of sentient beings, and of a life span arise along with it. Therefore the key to being free of the four marks is to be free of the mark of self. (For details see
A Detailed Explanation of the Diamond Sutra
In Eckhart Tolle’s
A New Earth (Awakening to Your Life’s Purpose)
, the structure, characteristics, and harm of the small self (the mark of self) are discussed in detail in modern language, and are worth consulting.
Master Guifeng says:

“All dharmas are like a dream—all the sages say so. Therefore deluded thoughts are originally quiescent, and the objects of dust are originally empty. This empty and still mind is luminously aware and not darkened. This empty and still knowing is your true nature. Let it be deluded or awakened, the mind knows itself; it does not depend on conditions to arise, nor does it come into being because of objects. The single word ‘knowing’
(the knowing of empty stillness)

is the gate of all wonders. Because of beginningless delusion, one deludedly clings to body and mind as I, and gives rise to thoughts of greed, hatred, and so on. If one meets a good friend who instructs one, one suddenly awakens to this empty and still knowing. This knowing is without thought and without form—who then is the mark of self or the mark of person? Awakening to all marks as empty, the mind of itself is without thought. When a thought arises, one is aware; being aware of it, it is gone. The wondrous gate of practice lies only here. Therefore, though one cultivates all practices, one takes no-thought as the teaching. When one attains the knowing and seeing of no-thought
(when one attains the knowing and seeing of no-thought)

, then love and hate naturally grow faint, compassion and wisdom naturally increase in clarity, karmic offenses are naturally cut off, and one’s practice naturally advances. Having understood that all marks are not marks, one naturally practices the practice of no-practice. When afflictions are exhausted, birth and death come to an end. When arising and ceasing have ceased, still illumination appears before one, functioning inexhaustibly, and this is named Buddha.”
(A General Preface to the Collected Interpretations of the Source of Chan)

[The single word ‘knowing’ is the gate of all wonders] This is to say: the knowing of empty stillness is the gate of all wonders. [Awakening to all marks as empty, the mind of itself is without thought. When a thought arises, one is aware; being aware of it, it is gone. The wondrous gate of practice lies only here] When you awaken to the fact that all marks are illusory, the mind of itself is without thought. If a deluded thought arises, you must at once awaken to the fact that this is taking the illusory as real and being turned by illusory marks. Once you awaken to this, the deluded thought vanishes at once. The wondrous gate of practice lies right here! [Being aware of it, it is gone] There are two methods for “being aware of it, it is gone”: first, as soon as you notice a deluded thought, at once stop it with the power of concentration; second, as soon as you notice a deluded thought, at once take the deluded thought as the material for contemplation: why did this deluded thought arise? What has it to do with me? Is there any need to think it through further? When you think it through deeply and thoroughly, the deluded thought ceases of itself (this is weakening and even uprooting the karmic seeds).
Therefore the knowing of empty stillness is the state of the original mind, while seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing are the state of the consciousness-mind.

When the self-nature is awakened, one takes the dharmakaya as oneself and the knowing of empty stillness as one’s own mind, and uses the physical body and thoughts as tools for practicing, for liberating sentient beings, and for handling the affairs of daily life.

[The knowing of empty stillness] The knowing of empty stillness is a knowing without knowing; to distinguish it from the mark-grasping knowing of seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing, it is also called “numinous knowing.” The Surangama Sutra says:
“When knowing and seeing establish a knowing, that is the root of ignorance; when knowing and seeing are without seeing, that is nirvana, pure and free of outflows.”
Master Hanshan’s Record of the Contemplation of the Lankavatara says:
“The mind being still and yet knowing, both true and false are left behind; this is named the self-awakened noble wisdom.”
For details see
the article “Mind, Self-Nature, and Tathagatagarbha”
The Platform Sutra of the Sixth Patriarch says:

“The self-nature can contain all dharmas, and is named the storehouse consciousness. If thinking arises, that is the turning consciousness; it produces the six consciousnesses, goes out through the six gates, and sees the six sense objects; thus the eighteen realms all arise and function from the self-nature. If the self-nature is deviant, eighteen deviant functions arise; if the self-nature is upright, eighteen upright functions arise. If the function is evil, it is the function of sentient beings; if the function is good, it is the function of the Buddha. From what does the function come? It comes from the self-nature.”

Translation: The self-nature can contain all dharmas, and so it is named the storehouse consciousness (the original nature). If the self-nature gives rise to thinking, that is the turning consciousness (the nature of consciousness), which produces the six consciousnesses (eye-consciousness, ear-consciousness, nose-consciousness, tongue-consciousness, body-consciousness, and mind-consciousness). The six consciousnesses go out through the six gates (that is, the six faculties: eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind) and see the six sense objects (form, sound, smell, taste, touch, and mental objects). Thus the eighteen realms (the six consciousnesses, six faculties, and six sense objects) are all the self-nature at work. If the self-nature is deviant, these eighteen realms give rise to eighteen deviant functions; if the self-nature is upright, these eighteen realms give rise to eighteen upright functions. If the function is evil, it is the function of sentient beings; if it is good, it is the function of the Buddha. From what does the function come? It comes from the self-nature.
(For details see
A Detailed Explanation of the Platform Sutra of the Sixth Patriarch

Therefore the self-nature has its deviant (deluded) and upright (awakened) aspects, and the thinker has evil and upright functions. Cultivation is precisely to turn the self-nature from delusion to awakening, until the great enlightenment. The Platform Sutra of the Sixth Patriarch says:
“When the self-nature is deluded, one is a sentient being; when the self-nature is awakened, one is a Buddha.”
When Shakyamuni Buddha, beneath the bodhi tree, saw the morning star at dawn and awakened to the Way, he said:
“How wondrous! How wondrous! All sentient beings are complete with the Tathagata’s wisdom and virtue marks, but because of deluded thinking and clinging they cannot realize them.”

The purpose of Chan inquiry—clarifying the mind and seeing the nature—is to remove the defilements of one’s own mind and truly see the original face of the self-nature. The defilements are deluded thinking and clinging; the original face of the self-nature is the Tathagata’s wisdom and virtue marks. If one is free of deluded thinking and clinging, one realizes one’s own Tathagata wisdom and virtue marks, and is a Buddha; otherwise one is a sentient being. Turning back to look at your own original face is simply not being hijacked by the deluded mind (the shadowy traces of the six sense objects), and thereby resting deluded thinking and clinging; and that resting is bodhi. In walking, standing, sitting, and lying down, in speech and silence, in movement and stillness, the work must be carried on without interruption, until the faculties and objects fall away and one thoroughly sees the original nature.

[Deluded clinging] To cling to things deludedly; here “clinging” is a verb. [But one who is free of deluded clinging is a Thus-Come One] One need only be free of deluded clinging, and one is the dharmakāya Buddha. The Laṅkāvatāra Sutra says: “The Dharma Buddha (the dharmakāya Buddha) is free of clinging.” The Diamond Sutra says: “Being free of all marks, one is named a Buddha.” [Thus-Come One] A Buddha awakened to the principle-substance of suchness; that is, the dharmakāya Buddha. The Laṅkāvatāra Sutra says: “What is a transformation Buddha? What is a reward-body Buddha? What is a Thus-Come One?”
The pith instruction of this method is:

Within, do not follow thoughts as they turn; without, do not be pulled by circumstances. Let no thought slip past; see every thought through. Take hold of no mark; abide in suchness, unmoved. Be free of deluded clinging, and you are a Thus-Come One.

Question: I know perfectly well that I am originally endowed with the Tathāgata’s wisdom and virtue, and that it is only because of deluded thinking and clinging that I cannot realize it. Yet why is it that when I strive with all my might to be free of deluded thinking and clinging, I still cannot shake them off?

Answer: Let us use the parable of the boxing champion to illustrate this principle vividly. A boxing champion famed throughout the world carelessly fell into drug addiction (a single thought of unenlightenment, and ignorance arises). His addiction grew ever stronger until he lost all his martial skill; he could not only no longer enter the ring, but was also cast aside by his “fans” and by public opinion. Having spent every last coin, he had no choice but to flee to a remote little town and take up company with beggars, living by begging and stealing. In his clearer moments he would recall his glorious record of victories and his wealth and honor, and again and again resolve to pull himself together and make a comeback; but the moment the craving struck, he could think of nothing else. At last he made up his mind: he would certainly break the addiction and return to the ring. He found a way to meet a most renowned physician and told him that he was the boxing champion so-and-so, told him the story of his downfall, and declared his determination to break the addiction and return to the ring. The physician shook his head and said to him: I sympathize deeply with what has befallen you, but your addiction is already deep-rooted; to break it is harder than to see God, and I am powerless to help. Dejected, he left the clinic and, on a park bench, interrogated himself over and over: could this be the end of his whole life? In the end he resolved to save himself. The process of withdrawal is desperately hard! When the craving struck, he wanted nothing but to go and take the drug. He bound himself to a post, and whether it felt as though ten thousand insects were boring into his heart, or as though his skull would split, his blood would freeze, and his body would burst, whatever the pain, the torment, and the craving (the temptation), he gritted his teeth and endured, passing through it again and again. Struggling and enduring without cease, persevering without cease, he at last broke the addiction. Then, working to make a living while training himself rigorously, he restored his strength and refined his craft. After three years of unflagging effort, he returned to the ring and won back his honor.
[Addiction] Addiction
means a repetitive compulsive behavior (obsessive-compulsive disorder) that continues to be repeated even when it is known that such behavior may bring harmful consequences.

In this parable, deluded thinking and clinging is taking the drug (taking part in the virtual game that is the world of appearances). And our ceaseless drug-taking since beginningless kalpas has made our addiction (addiction to deluded thinking and clinging) deep-rooted. What we must now do is like breaking the addiction and restoring our martial skill, returning to the ring, and becoming champion once more. When you say, “I strive with all my might to be free of deluded thinking and clinging, yet I cannot shake them off,” that is like the clearer moments in the parable when he wanted to make a comeback (to return to the source and restore the original): it is the call from the depths of his heart. But if one truly means to return to the source and restore the original, one must also, with both feet on the ground, break the addiction through practice (utterly let go of deluded thinking and clinging) and so fully restore one’s martial skill (the Tathāgata’s wisdom and virtue).

Practice constantly faces crossroads and the challenge of an addiction (addiction to deluded thinking and clinging) that flares up again and again. The self-nature seeks liberation while the physical body seeks pleasure; which way to go depends on your wisdom in choosing the right road and your perseverance in holding to right practice
, and strong self-motivation and unremitting self-improvement are the prerequisites for success.

[Perseverance] Perseverance is governing oneself with an unshakable will: excellence in work comes from diligence, and it is ruined by play. What should be done, do resolutely and do well; what should not be done, resolutely do not do, without the slightest hesitation. Perseverance is passion and striving toward a long-range goal, an enduring and lasting tenacity, your persistence toward the future, day after day, until your dream becomes reality. (Please watch
The Key to Success—Perseverance (video)
) [Self-motivation] Self-motivation refers to the psychological trait by which an individual, needing no external reward or punishment as an incentive, can work hard of himself toward a set goal.

Practice has proved that a practitioner must, through his own cultivation and training, possess excellent psychological qualities if he is to win victories in the actual combat against deluded thinking and clinging.
Finely looking back at the thinker is also an excellent way to investigate Chan.
Question: How does one look back at the thinker?

Answer: Whenever the thinker is about to indulge in deluded thinking, say to it: “Fine, you want to indulge in deluded thinking; I will simply watch how you think.” (It does not matter that deluded thoughts arise; what matters is that you watch how they think. As a thought arises, be aware of it; be aware and not deluded.) Then just watch how it thinks. As a result, it finds itself unable to think. (If it really can still think, then write down every thought it thinks!) When the thinker can no longer think, keep on observing it, always observing it, to see what else it will do. Whatever it wants to do, you watch from the far shore, watching without judging. Do not slacken; whether walking, standing, sitting, or lying down, keep observing in this way. In time, the thinker produces fewer and fewer thoughts, and then a light awareness is all that is needed. If a deluded thought arises, one stark moment of awareness, and with that awareness it is gone. Later, even awareness is not needed, and one enters silent illumination. When the time and conditions ripen, when the melon is ripe it drops from the stem, at a touch or a bump, one suddenly has a great awakening and thoroughly sees the original nature.
[Silent illumination]

At this point, although awareness is no longer raised, its illumination remains, illumining naturally; this is called silent illumination. Master Dayu’s verse says: “Silent illumination illumines silence; above all, do not use force. To become a Buddha and be your own master, there is no other secret.”
Question: When looking back at the thinker, what should one do if deluded thoughts keep circling and will not leave?

Answer: These deluded thoughts are karmic seeds of deeply knotted emotional roots coming into activity. That deluded thoughts keep circling shows that the enemy (the karmic seeds) is strong and I (the power of awareness) am weak. While striving to strengthen awareness, one should also weaken and even uproot these karmic seeds, gradually bringing it about that I am strong and the enemy weak, that I grow stronger and stronger and the enemy weaker and weaker. The deluded thoughts that keep circling provide precisely the opportunity to weaken and uproot these karmic seeds. One must at once raise the wisdom of contemplation: when the deviant comes, deliver it with the right; when delusion comes, deliver it with awakening; when folly comes, deliver it with wisdom; when evil comes, deliver it with good. Think the principle through deeply, thoroughly, and to the bottom; remove the matter by means of the principle; uphold practice by means of strength. Take hold of no mark; abide in suchness, unmoved; turn karma with mind. Lu You’s poem says: “What comes from paper is, after all, shallow; only when you have truly done the thing yourself do you know it through and through.” These are words from the heart. This book has set forth many principles and methods for countering deluded thinking and clinging; only by practicing them in person,
by countering them

can you comprehend the wonder within them, and only then can they become your own principles and methods. Comprehend in actual combat, apply in actual combat, bring into play in actual combat—the joy is endless!
Question: What is the relation between the thinker and the self-nature?
Answer: The thinker is simply the consciousness-mind of the self-nature; the nature is the substance, the mind is the function. On self-nature and consciousness-mind, see in detail
Mind, Self-Nature, and Tathāgatagarbha

The presence-mind-watching taught in the previous section, “returning to the one,” is also an excellent way to investigate. When the state of watching the mind without thoughts has already become quite stable, there is no need to watch the mind attentively any longer;

then a light awareness is all that is needed. If a deluded thought arises, one stark moment of awareness, and with that awareness it is gone. Later, even awareness is not needed, and one enters silent illumination.

Investigating what the present thought is—this too is an excellent way to investigate. If a deluded thought arises, watch how it means to act. Resolve to see the matter to the bottom, all the way to the place where there is no thought. Gather your mental strength and press the inquiry closely: whether a good thought or an evil thought, whoever comes, cut it down. Any deluded thought, pressed in this way, is at once shattered, until it is utterly melted away and leaves no trace. When the state of no-thought has already become quite stable, there is no need to keep investigating what the present thought is; then a light awareness is all that is needed. If a deluded thought arises, one stark moment of awareness, and with that awareness it is gone. Later, even awareness is not needed, and one enters silent illumination.
Looking back within and illumining inward is also an excellent way to investigate. Master Hanshan gave this instruction:

“Only in daily activity, at the place where mind has not yet stirred and thought has not yet arisen, plant your feet firmly and look back within, illumining inward. At the place where a single thought arises, at once pursue and examine this one thought: from where does it arise? Pursuing it to the place where the single thought arises, you find it is originally unborn; then all deluded thoughts and emotional calculations melt away on the spot. What must be avoided, however, is lacking the power of courage, so that you cannot seize the throat of it; unaware, the thoughts continue in succession, and you flow on without returning.”
(Mengyou ji,
“Instruction to Xiao Xuanpu, President of the Ministry of Rites”)

Translation: Only amid daily affairs, at the place where mind has not yet stirred and thought has not yet arisen, plant your feet firmly (abide in the state of no-thought) and look back within, illumining inward. Whenever a thought arises, at once pursue and examine this one thought: from where does it arise? Pursuing it to the place where the single thought arises, you find it is originally unborn; then all deluded thoughts and emotional calculations melt away on the spot. What must be avoided (what one fears), however, is lacking the power of courage, being unable to seize the throat of it (the vital point, namely the place where the single thought arises), losing awareness and letting deluded thoughts continue in succession, and so falling into deluded thinking, unable to extricate oneself.
[The place where a single thought arises] The moment a single thought first arises.
Turning the hearing back to the self-nature is also an excellent way to investigate: turning the hearing back to the self-nature densely and without interruption,
so that whether walking, standing, sitting, or lying down, one takes good care of the practice and does not let it be lost.

As the days pass and the practice deepens, when the melon is ripe it drops from the stem; when the time and conditions come, at a touch or a bump, one suddenly has a great awakening (thoroughly seeing the original nature). (See in detail
The Method of Perfect Penetration through the Ear-Faculty
The Shurangama Sutra,
“Chapter on Perfect Penetration through the Ear-Faculty,” says:
“Turning the hearing back to hear the self-nature, the nature accomplishes the unsurpassed Way.”

[The nature accomplishes the unsurpassed Way] The self-nature is transformed from the state of consciousness-nature into the state of original nature (returning to the source and restoring the original) and thereby perfectly realizes the fruit of Buddhahood. [The unsurpassed Way] The Way attained by the Tathāgata, beyond which there is nothing higher; hence it is called the unsurpassed Way. The Lotus Sutra says: “Each one thinks thus: by what means shall I cause living beings to enter the unsurpassed Way and quickly accomplish the Buddha-body?”
Turning inward to accord with the self-nature,
is also an excellent way to investigate: densely and without interruption
turning inward to accord with the self-nature
, so that whether walking, standing, sitting, or lying down, one takes good care of the practice and does not let it be lost.

As the days pass and the practice deepens, when the melon is ripe it drops from the stem; when the time and conditions come, at a touch or a bump, one suddenly has a great awakening (thoroughly seeing the original nature).
Question: How does one accord with the self-nature?
Answer: The self-nature is the inner spiritual energy (see in detail
Mind, Self-Nature, and Tathāgatagarbha

). To accord with the self-nature is to be aware of it, feel it, and become one with it. For sentient beings, the body is the dwelling of the self-nature. The Platform Sutra of the Sixth Patriarch says:
“The physical body is a house.”
Patriarch Linji says:
“Just look at the puppets on the stage; all their pulling and tugging depends entirely on the man inside.”
This says that the physical body is like a wooden puppet, and what manipulates this physical body is the self-nature. Hence the Juexin Jue (Formula for Cultivating the Mind) says:
“When the hundred bones crumble and scatter, they return to fire and wind; one thing remains ever numinous, covering heaven and covering earth.”

Throughout the twelve periods of the day, knowing hunger and knowing thirst, knowing cold and knowing heat, being angry or being pleased—this is the self-nature. The physical body is a compound of the four conditions of earth, water, fire, and wind; its substance is insentient and without feeling. How could it see, hear, sense, and know? What can see, hear, sense, and know must be your self-nature. The patriarch says:

“The four elements do not understand how to expound the Dharma or listen to the Dharma; empty space does not understand how to expound the Dharma or listen to the Dharma. Only that which before your eyes is vividly and solitarily clear, without form or shape, understands how to expound the Dharma and listen to the Dharma. That which is called formless and shapeless
(that which has no form)
is your self-nature.”
The Mahāyāna Laṅkāvatāra Sutra says:
“It is like a wooden man or a raised corpse
(causing a corpse to rise and walk about)
, which by the power of the piśāca’s mechanism moves, turns, and acts without cease
(acts without stopping)

This says: the physical body is like a wooden man or a corpse, moving by the power of a mechanism. This mechanism is the self-nature, this life-force. To accord with the self-nature means to feel this living vitality within the body, to become one with it, and to abide in it. If you maintain accord with the self-nature, floating thoughts do not arise, and you can easily and naturally achieve single-minded focus, and even no-thought. To accord with the self-nature densely and without interruption means that at all times and in all places you are aware of and feel the living vitality of the self-nature within the body, become one with it, and abide in it. In daily life, when conditions come, give; when conditions go, be still. Whether doing things or conversing, always maintain accord with the self-nature, free and autonomous (not falling into deluded thinking, not manipulated by circumstances). The Platform Sutra of the Sixth Patriarch says:
“Not departing from the self-nature is itself the field of blessing.”

[Not departing from the self-nature is itself the field of blessing] When one accords with the self-nature, one no longer deludedly clings to the five aggregates of body and mind as “I”; rather, the master within is in charge—this is the greatest field of blessing.

Ordinarily, what people never let go of is the “I” of the five aggregates of body and mind; this is the state of delusion. When you depart from that “I” and accord with the self-nature, this is the state of clear awareness. Not departing from the “I” of the five aggregates of body and mind is creating the karma of saṃsāra; departing from that “I” and according with the self-nature is cultivating the field of blessing and constantly giving rise to wisdom. The Juexin Jue says:
“One who awakens to this and guards it sits in oneness and is unmoved and liberated; one who is deluded about this and turns away from it goes to the six destinies and endures kalpa-long saṃsāra.”
The concrete steps for practicing accord with the self-nature are:
First step: become able to perceive clearly that your inner being is a single field of energy.
Second step: focus completely on this feeling.
Third step: bring your attention more deeply into this feeling, become one with it, merge with the energy field, and remain there as long as possible.
In this way you are freed from forms and from the shackles of identifying with forms, freed from
the “I” of the five aggregates of body and mind,
and are placed in a state of deep stillness and peace that is yet full of joy and vitality. Awareness of the inner energy field enables you to remain present and to abide in the present moment.
At the beginning you may do this practice with the eyes closed; once the practice is familiar, gradually move on to doing it with the eyes open as well.
According with the nature while watching the mind is especially effective. The method is: accord with the self-nature and watch the present thought

If a deluded thought arises, this shows that the accord has been interrupted; then rouse your spirits and once again attentively accord and watch, and the deluded thought ceases of itself. Once the practice of according with the nature while watching the mind is proficient, one moves on to awareness and illumination, illumining gently. If a deluded thought arises, one stark moment of awareness, and it leaves no trace. When the practice of awareness and illumination is proficient, like cold fire drawing out smoke in one unbroken thread, then let the body drop away, release the hands and let them range freely, and enter silent illumination. When the time and conditions come, when the melon is ripe it drops from the stem, at a touch or a bump, one suddenly has a great awakening and thoroughly sees the original nature.

The essential point of doing the practice is: make according with the nature while watching the mind focused, continuous, and sustained. And one must firmly guard the gate against deluded thoughts: let no thought slip past (do not be deceived by it), see every thought through (do not be shrouded by it, do not follow and be toyed with by it, do not take it as something real).
Old Master Xuyun’s method of investigating Chan is:
to investigate toward the place before a single thought has sprouted:
The so-called
huatou

is the moment before a single thought has arisen; the instant a thought arises, it has already become the tail of the word. This moment before a single thought has arisen is called non-arising; not being scattered, not being torpid, not dwelling in stillness, not falling into emptiness, is called non-ceasing.
(A single thought not arising, awareness not ceasing.)
Moment by moment, with this single bare thought, reflecting the light back upon this ‘non-arising and non-ceasing’—this is called
watching the huatou

, or taking care of the huatou.” “You must know that the true huatou is to be investigated toward the place before a single thought has sprouted. Not distinguishing movement from stillness, thought after thought without interval—this is called
the feeling of doubt
(Not distinguishing movement from stillness, investigating toward the place before a single thought has sprouted, thought after thought without interval—this is called the feeling of doubt.)
(See in detail the earlier chapter “The Head of the Word (Xuyun’s Chan Method)”).
Question: “To investigate toward the place before a single thought has sprouted”—how does one investigate?
Answer: Reflect the light back upon this ‘non-arising and non-ceasing.’
Therefore, investigation is simply this:
reflecting the light back upon this ‘non-arising and non-ceasing.’
As for how to do the work of investigation, Chan Master Mengshan Deyi set us a shining example; see in detail
The Chan Method of Dahui
, in the chapter “Awakening.”
Question: How can one become a single piece?
Answer: On this, Master Hanshan gave this instruction:
“If you truly can apply the mind, work solely at the place before a single thought arises
(investigate toward the place before a single thought has sprouted)

. After a long time, when it is utterly familiar, a single thought does not arise and the original substance appears before you. The constant light is perfectly clear, unchanged through brightness and darkness, movement and stillness are one suchness—only then is it becoming a single piece.”
(Mengyou ji,
“Reply to the Monk Haiyin of Huzhou”)

blocks.text: Chapter Four: Breaking Through the Three Barriers

inline.s: The three barriers of the Chan gate are the three stages of sudden awakening and gradual cultivation in the Chan school: the initial barrier, the heavy (
chóng

) barrier, and the firm barrier. 1. Investigating the huatou draws forth leak-free wisdom; by means of leak-free wisdom one understands one’s own original mind and sees one’s own original nature. This is called breaking the initial barrier, also called breaking the root investigation. 2. Once one has seen the nature, one then uses leak-free wisdom to counter affliction, until affliction is subdued and no longer comes into activity; this is called breaking the heavy barrier. 3. Yet the subduing of affliction still depends on the effort of countering it; only when affliction is utterly purified, so that one acts spontaneously and without effort, does one penetrate the firm barrier.
Among the three
barriers, breaking the initial barrier is sudden awakening, while breaking the heavy barrier and the firm barrier is gradual cultivation.
Seeing one’s own original nature (seeing the nature)

Since ancient times there has been the saying “direct pointing to seeing the nature.” But in order to let Chan practitioners develop the capacity to break the heavy barrier and the firm barrier, Awareness Chan still opens up the original through the ten thousand thoughts returning to one, the one returning to no-thing, and cutting, cutting investigation
[Direct pointing to seeing the nature

] For example, Damei asked Mazu, ‘What is Buddha?’ The Patriarch said, ‘Mind itself is Buddha!’ At these words Damei had a great awakening (he saw his own original nature). Again, Lingxun asked Master Guizong, ‘What is Buddha?’ Guizong said, ‘Were I now to tell you, I fear you would not believe it!’ Lingxun said, ‘The Master’s words are sincere; how would I dare not believe!’ Guizong said, ‘You yourself are it!’ At these words Lingxun had an insight (he saw his own original nature).

[Leak-free] Pure, without affliction. “Leak” is another name for affliction. [Subduing affliction] The effort of countering is present, and affliction does not come into activity; this is called subduing affliction. [Cutting off affliction] One acts spontaneously without effort, and affliction does not come into activity; this is called cutting off affliction.
To investigate Chan is to break through the three barriers, see the nature, subdue affliction, and cut off affliction
, so as to end birth and death and leave the three realms. Master Hanshan says:

“The ancients who investigated and sought took their stand only at the crossroads of birth and death, seeking what is certain and ultimate; they did not, apart from this, take paper, ink, and written words, or the three vehicles and twelve divisions of the teachings, as some marvelous special thing.”
(Mengyou ji, · “Instruction to the Seat-Master Miaozhan”)

Afflictions are thousand upon thousand and ten thousand upon ten thousand, but summed up they are the three poisons: greed, anger, and delusion. After seeing the nature (breaking the initial barrier), one must cultivate in dependence on the nature, doing the work of guarding and of letting be, in order to extinguish the three poisons. The work of guarding is subduing affliction (breaking the heavy barrier), while the work of letting be is cutting off affliction (penetrating the firm barrier).

In subduing affliction and cutting off affliction, one should be present as much as possible, so that awareness is ever before one. For when one is present, there is no affliction; and even if affliction occasionally arises through a slip, one can become aware of it in time and extinguish it on the spot.
After awakening (seeing the nature),

cultivation has two stages, guarding and letting be: 1. Guarding. Protect the mind, do not run after circumstances, so as to subdue affliction. 2. Letting be. Let the mind act spontaneously, do not run after circumstances, so as to cut off affliction.

The first stage is protecting the mind (not giving rise to a mind that dwells on form, sound, odor, taste, touch, or mental objects); when the work of protection is mature, one then drops the protection and drops the constraint, and does the work of letting be, letting the mind act spontaneously and without effort yet still not overstep the rule (giving rise to a mind that dwells on nothing). The “rule” here is non-greed, non-anger, and non-delusion. Taking breaking the drug addiction as an analogy: the first stage is the stage of protection, which is to recognize deeply the harm of taking drugs and to keep strictly apart from the drug. Those with a severe addiction may even need to train for a time in a rehabilitation center, where under a strict environment and discipline they learn certain methods and acquire a basic ability to break the addiction, before returning home to continue breaking it by way of protection. Once the work of protection is mature, one must begin the work of the second stage, letting be. One must reach the point where, though the drug lies within reach at one’s side, one is not tempted, and one works and lives as normal. Another example: the Master said, “Subdue the self and return to propriety.” He also said, “Follow what the heart desires without overstepping the rule.” Here, “subduing the self and returning to propriety” is the work of guarding, and “following what the heart desires without overstepping the rule” is the state of letting be. Through doing the work of “subduing the self and returning to propriety,” after decades of effort, Confucius at seventy attained the state of “following what the heart desires without overstepping the rule.”
The Diamond Sutra says:

“All bodhisattvas and mahāsattvas should thus give rise to a pure mind: they should not give rise to a mind dwelling on form, they should not give rise to a mind dwelling on sound, odor, taste, touch, or mental objects; they should give rise to a mind that dwells on nothing.”
The Diamond Sutra also says:

“They should not give rise to a mind dwelling on form, they should not give rise to a mind dwelling on sound, odor, taste, touch, or mental objects; they should give rise to a mind that dwells on nothing.”

In these two passages of scripture, not giving rise to a mind dwelling on form, sound, odor, taste, touch, or mental objects is the stage of guarding; giving rise to a mind that dwells on nothing (giving rise to a mind that dwells on nothing) is the stage of letting be—what is called “passing through a thicket of ten thousand flowers, not a single leaf clings to the body.” The Sutra of Perfect Enlightenment says:
“Good sons! All bodhisattvas and all living beings in the final age should, at all times, not give rise to deluded thoughts
(not giving rise to a mind dwelling on form, sound, odor, taste, touch, or mental objects)
, and yet should not extinguish those deluded minds either
(giving rise to a mind that dwells on nothing)

; dwelling in the realm of deluded thoughts, they should not add knowing, and toward that non-knowing they should not dispute over the real. When those living beings hear this Dharma door, believe, understand, accept, and uphold it, and do not give rise to alarm or fear, they are then named as following the awakened nature.”
The core of both stages, guarding and letting be, is the removal of habitual tendencies.

There are three methods for removing habitual tendencies: removal by way of things, removal by way of principle, and removal by way of mind. Removal by way of things is to correct oneself in the midst of affairs. Removal by way of things means forcing oneself outwardly not to transgress; its difficulty is far greater than removing from within, and moreover the root of the illness always remains, so that when the east is extinguished the west arises—this is not a way to uproot habitual tendencies thoroughly. One who is skilled at removing habitual tendencies will, before prohibiting a thing, first make the principle clear; once the principle is clear and one removes in accordance with principle, the habitual tendency will not reappear. Removal by way of mind is to remove from the mind. Though habitual tendencies are of a thousand and ten thousand kinds, all arise from the mind; if one does not give rise to mind by clinging to circumstances, habitual tendencies dissolve of themselves. Its key point is: within, do not follow thoughts as they turn; without, do not be pulled by circumstances. For these three kinds of removal, one may refer to the section “Three Methods of Correcting Faults” in Liaofan’s Four Lessons (see in detail
Annotated Liaofan’s Four Lessons

blocks.text: 1. Breaking the Initial Barrier (Breaking the Root Investigation)

inline.s: As said earlier, the instruction on investigating Chan and seeing the original face appears in the Platform Sutra of the Sixth Patriarch. The Sixth Patriarch instructed Huiming:
“Not thinking of good, not thinking of evil, at just this moment, which
(what)
is the original face of Upāsaka Ming?”
At these words Huiming had a great awakening.

“Not thinking of good, not thinking of evil, at just this moment” is the moment before a single thought has arisen. “Which (what) is the original face of Upāsaka Ming” is precisely reflecting the light back: what is the original face? Therefore the method of seeing one’s own original nature is: at the moment before a single thought has arisen, reflect the light back: what is the original face?
Master Hanshan says:
“When the night air is clear, gather the mind and sit upright, look back within and illumine inward; where it is utterly still and yet not dark, you will see the original face for yourself.”
(Mengyou ji,
“Instruction to the Student Chen Zifu”)

Question: Why does the above interpret the Sixth Patriarch’s last sentence, “that is the original face of Upāsaka Ming,” an affirmative statement, as a question: “Which (what) is the original face of Upāsaka Ming?”

Answer: Because in ancient Chinese, “that” has two meanings: 1. It points to a more distant time, place, or thing, as opposed to “this”; it is a demonstrative. 2. It is the same as “which,” a interrogative. Therefore “that” in this instruction of the Sixth Patriarch has always been viewed in two ways: 1. “That” in “that is the original face of Upāsaka Ming” is a demonstrative, indicating that the moment when not a single thought arises is the original face. 2. “That” in “that is the original face of Upāsaka Ming” is the interrogative “which.” On this, Old Master Xuyun wrote in “Two Replies to Upāsaka Jin Hongshu (1948)”: “Your letter says: ‘Simply put everything down, think of neither good nor evil, and contemplate in just this way; that is it. There is no need to do the work of investigation, which differs from watching the huatou.’ Please do not misunderstand the Sixth Patriarch’s words to Huiming—‘not thinking of good, not thinking of evil, at just this moment, that is the original face of Upāsaka Ming’—as an affirmative statement. The latter sentence is in fact a question; the point of focus lies just here, and you must be most careful. (Upāsaka Jin Hongshu notes: As for the two characters ‘that,’ both Chan Master Huangbo and National Master Yulin render them as ‘how,’ so that it is an interrogative admits of no further doubt.) If not thinking of good and not thinking of evil were itself it, one would already have fallen into the annihilationist heresy!”
Regarding this instruction of the Sixth Patriarch on seeing one’s own original nature, Mr. Liu Shuyuan says in The Essentials of the Buddhadharma:
“Bodhidharma’s three phrases
(‘Externally, cease all conditions; internally, the mind has no panting; let the mind be like a wall’)

sum up everything. The Sixth Patriarch’s ‘not thinking of good, not thinking of evil’ is ‘externally, cease all conditions.’ ‘At just this moment’ is ‘internally, the mind has no panting.’ The wording differs, but how could there be two meanings? To reach ‘at just this moment’ is simply to be unmoved in one flavor; do it on and on, one thought for ten thousand years—what further Dharma is there? ‘Which
(what)
is the original face of Upāsaka Ming?’ is a question; this is called setting the trigger in motion.

(Note in the original: In the teachings this is called the constant trigger. The Buddhadharma takes the mind as the trigger, hence the saying: ‘One thought turning back to the trigger, and one is the same as the original attainment.’)

The Chan gate says: For an ordinary person the mysterious gate is tightly shut, and the lock of consciousness is hard to open. The trigger is the mysterious gate; the superior one casts a single phrase at it, strikes the trigger into motion, and he awakens at once. Yet what matters most in this public case is the three characters ‘at just this moment’
(note in the original: that is, the moment of not thinking of good or evil)

, which is the secret of the Chan school. If one who has aroused the mind can abide in the mind in this way, awakening is not far off. The patriarch says: ‘At just this moment is called the time before the Buddha was born.’ It is also called: ‘Sitting on the summit, precious beyond measure.’ Only when one can abide in the mind thus for several hours a day does one accord with the method. There will naturally be the causal condition of the trigger being set in motion; there is no need for anyone to guide one. The patriarch says: ‘If only one can be at just this moment, there is no fear of not awakening thoroughly.’ This belongs to the secret essentials of the mind-dharma, and can be practiced with strength.”

[Bodhidharma’s three phrases] These are the first three phrases of Patriarch Bodhidharma’s instruction to the Second Patriarch Huike: “Externally, cease all conditions; internally, the mind has no panting; let the mind be like a wall—thus may one enter the Way.” [The mysterious gate] Broadly, a door or gateway; also the gate by which one enters the Way.

Patriarch Bodhidharma’s instruction means: externally, cease clinging; internally, let the mind not give rise to thoughts; let the mind be like a wall, not giving rise to discrimination—that is to say, circumstances cannot move the mind; thus, and only thus, may one enter the Way. Of these four phrases, the last is the fruit; the work is done only on the first three.
Therefore the essential purport of investigating Chan and entering the Way is:
externally, cease all conditions; internally, the mind has no panting; let the mind be like a wall.
In the Sutra of the Buddha’s Treasury, the Buddha says:
“The Buddhas’ anuttarā-samyak-saṃbodhi is wholly without thought and without mental activity.”
In the Shurangama Sutra, the Buddha says:
“All living beings, from beginningless time, continue in birth and death solely because they do not know the permanently abiding true mind, the pure and luminous substance of the nature
(it is entirely because they do not know the pure and luminous substance of the nature, the true mind that permanently abides)
, and instead employ deluded thoughts
(and go off using deluded thoughts)
; these thoughts are not real, and so there is turning about in saṃsāra.”
The Awakening of Faith says:
“One who is free of the marks of thought is equal to the realm of empty space.”
The Essentials of Mind-Transmission says:
“Cease thought, forget calculation, and the Buddha appears of himself before you.”
The Sixth Patriarch says:

“If you wish to know the essentials of the mind, simply do not think of good or evil at all, and you will naturally enter the pure mind-substance, utterly still and eternally silent, with marvelous function as numberless as the sands of the Ganges.”
(Platform Sutra of the Sixth Patriarch)
[Purity of nature and luminous substance] “Purity of nature”: the nature is originally pure, without bondage or defilement. “Luminous substance”: the substance that is luminous and wondrous.
Chan Master Linji
(Linji Yixuan of Zhenzhou in the Tang dynasty, heir of Huangbo, founder of the Linji school)
ascended the hall and said:
“On the lump of red flesh there is an unranked true person, who constantly comes and goes through the gates of your faces. Those who have not yet realized it
(those who have not yet seen the nature)
look, look.”
(Wudeng Huiyuan)
The Xu Chuandeng Lu records:
Yu Daopo was a woman of Jinling who sold fried glutinous rice cakes
(a kind of fried glutinous rice food)
for a living. She often
(the character means “once,” “formerly”)
went along with the assembly to inquire and question Langya
(Chan Master Huijue Guangzhao of Mount Langya in Chuzhou; “Langya” is also written “Langya (láng yá)”)

, and Langya showed her Linji’s words about the unranked true person. One day she heard a beggar singing the Lotus Song: ‘Were it not that Liu Yi carried the letter, by what cause could he have entered Lake Dongting
(were it not for seeing the unranked true person, by what cause could one see the original face)
?’ Suddenly she had a great awakening and threw her cake tray to the ground. Her husband, looking askance, said, ‘Are you mad
(have you gone crazy)
?’ Daopo slapped him and said
(Yu Daopo gave him a slap and said)
: ‘This is not your realm.’ She went to see Langya. Langya looked at her and knew her attainment. He asked: ‘Which
(what)
is the unranked true person?’ Daopo answered at once: ‘There is an unranked one, with six arms and three heads, striving in anger; with one split he opens Mount Hua into two roads
(with all his strength splitting open the shell of ignorance, the dharmakāya appears at once)
, and the waters of ten thousand years do not know spring.’ From this her fame grew abundant
(in the manner of flourishing)
and widespread.”

[Lotus Song] Also called the lotus fall. A kind of narrative song, beaten in rhythm with bamboo clappers, each section often ending with a refrain or coda of lines like “lotus fall, fall lotus.” [Were it not that Liu Yi carried the letter] This is an inverted sentence used to strengthen the tone; the meaning is: Liu Yi would not have carried the letter. [Liu Yi carries the letter] The story comes from the Tang tale “The Story of Liu Yi”: in the second year of Yifeng under Emperor Gaozong of Tang, Liu Yi failed the examinations, and on his way to visit a friend in Jinghe County he saw a woman herding sheep on the bank of the Jing River. The shepherdess looked sorrowful and seemed to be waiting for something. Liu Yi wondered and asked her, and learned that the woman was the daughter of the Dragon King of Lake Dongting and the wife of the little dragon of the Jing River. The little dragon of the Jing River was coarse and foolish, and was bewitched by maidservants; husband and wife were at odds, and the dragon girl was punished to herd sheep on the bank of the Jing River in suffering. Hearing this, Liu Yi’s blood stirred and he felt deep sympathy, and so he accepted the dragon girl’s entrusting and carried her family letter to the dragon palace of Lake Dongting. When the dragon girl’s uncle, the fire dragon of Qiantang, learned of this, he flew into a rage and led his water troops to the Jing River, swallowed the little dragon of the Jing River alive, and rescued the dragon girl. [With six arms and three heads, striving in anger] “Six arms and three heads” describes the unranked true person’s vast spiritual powers and extraordinary abilities. “Anger” means to open the eyes wide. For example: to glare. [With one split he opens Mount Hua into two roads] Li Bai’s “Song of the Cloud Terrace of the Western Peak” says: “The giant spirit roars and splits the two mountains; the surging waves spout and shoot toward the Eastern Sea.” Legend says that Mount Taihua and Mount Shaohua were originally one mountain, facing the Yellow River, and when the river’s waters passed it they could only flow by a detour. The god of the Yellow River, the giant spirit, was indignant; with his hand he split the summit and with his foot he kicked apart the mountain’s base, dividing the mountain into two so that the river waters could pass straight through. Here, “with one split he opens Mount Hua into two roads” means: with all one’s strength splitting open the shell of ignorance, the dharmakāya appears at once. [The waters of ten thousand years do not know spring] The waters of ten thousand years do not know spring, summer, autumn, or winter. This means: acting spontaneously and freely, mind and circumstances having nothing to do with each other.
Master Hanshan’s Mengyou ji, “Instruction to the Chan Person Liaoxin Hai,” says:

“Simply look, thought after thought, at the place where thought has not yet arisen. By dwelling in this one point of being free of thought, after a long time the stream of thought suddenly breaks off, mind and circumstances are both forgotten, and you are like a lion slipped from its rope, roaming freely.”
Question: It is recorded that Master Yuexi asked the monk Tieyan: “By what method should one apply effort so as to understand the mind and see the nature?” The monk Tieyan replied:

“You must not go and cut off deluded thoughts; use the eye-faculty to look back toward that place which neither abides in existence nor in nothingness, the deep dark pit, whether walking, standing, sitting, or lying down, without interruption. When the time and conditions come, and with a huo the vast dark pit of ignorance breaks open, then you can understand the mind and see the nature.

The Master (Master Yuexi), hearing these words, was as though drinking sweet dew, and from then on applied effort day and night, bitterly investigating, until his countenance grew haggard and he was thin as firewood. Then one midnight, hearing the sound of the wind blowing the leaves of the wutong tree outside the window, he suddenly had an insight.” Why did the monk Tieyan say, “You must not go and cut off deluded thoughts”?

Answer: The key point of the method the monk Tieyan instructed is: “Use the eye-faculty to look back toward that place which neither abides in existence nor in nothingness, the deep dark pit, whether walking, standing, sitting, or lying down,
without interruption

.” What “you must not go and cut off deluded thoughts” means is: you should not place your attention on cutting off deluded thoughts, but should place it wholly and completely on looking back. In fact, so long as you look back attentively and continuously, deluded thoughts cease of themselves. Moreover, so long as you go on looking back attentively and continuously, no deluded thought will arise again. If a deluded thought does arise, this shows that the looking back has been interrupted through slackening; therefore do not go and cut off the deluded thought either, but rouse your spirits and once again look back attentively and continuously, and the deluded thought ceases of itself. So the key point of effort in this method is: attentively, continuously, and persistently “use the eye-faculty to look back toward that place which neither abides in existence nor in nothingness, the deep dark pit, whether walking, standing, sitting, or lying down,
without interruption
.” As the days pass and the practice deepens, when the melon is ripe it drops from the stem, and with a single huo the deep dark pit breaks open, and one thoroughly sees the nature.

[Whether walking, standing, sitting, or lying down, without interruption] The “without interruption” spoken of here means not only that one should not stop the looking back, but that even while looking back one should be focused and continuous, and must not let there be an interruption through slackening.
The Tang-dynasty nun Wujinzang’s “Poem on Awakening to the Way” says:
“All day I sought spring and did not see spring; my straw sandals wore through the clouds on the ridge. Returning, I chanced to sniff a plum blossom
(a single thought turning back the light, a sudden awakening)
, and spring was already ten parts upon the branch
(so she had long since seen the nature! It was only that no clear-eyed one had, at the right moment, pointed it out)
Xin Qiji’s “The Green Jade Cup: The Lantern Festival” says:
“In the crowd I sought her a thousand times and a hundred; then, suddenly
turning my head, there she was, where the lantern light was dim.”
[Suddenly
(mò)
] Indicates an action brought on by some scene. [The lantern light was dim] The lantern light was about to go out.
After seeing the nature, one should often enter and abide in the state of seeing the nature, making seeing the nature one’s daily fare. The Fifth Patriarch Hongren says:
“One who has seen the nature must see it at the words
to speak of seeing is at once to see
. If one is like this, then even wheeling a blade and charging into battle, one still sees it.”

(Platform Sutra of the Sixth Patriarch) Having, in seeing the nature, experientially realized the innately possessed awakened nature, one must go further and guard and sustain the awakened nature, so that it is ever present, and polish and test it amid circumstances and conditions. Let go of all deluded thoughts and discrimination, so that this one thought of awakened nature can be clear, lucid, and abiding in suchness, unmoved; guard and sustain it continuously, and one will certainly be able to “stand firm” and “stand long,” and even attain something.
[At the words] Beneath a single word; instantly.
Breaking the initial barrier (breaking the root investigation) spoken of here is what the Platform Sutra of the Sixth Patriarch calls “seeing one’s own original nature”
when both coarse thoughts and subtle thoughts have ceased (that is, what is ordinarily called no-thought) and one
experientially realizes the mind-substance of no-thought
What Patriarch Bodhidharma first transmitted to the Second Patriarch Huike was precisely this mind-substance of no-thought.
“The Patriarch
(Bodhidharma)

at first dwelt at Shaolin Temple for nine years, and in teaching the Dharma to the Second Patriarch he only taught: ‘Externally, cease all conditions; internally, the mind has no panting; let the mind be like a wall—thus may one enter the Way.’ Huike spoke of mind and nature in many ways
(the wondrous substance of the true mind)
, but never once accorded with the principle; the Patriarch only blocked what was wrong in them
(Patriarch Bodhidharma only negated his answers)
, and did not explain to him
the mind-substance of no-thought
(did not plainly tell him that the answer was the mind-substance of no-thought)
. Huike suddenly said: ‘I have ceased all conditions
(I have ceased all manner of clinging)
.’ The Patriarch said: ‘Are you not becoming annihilated?’ Huike said: ‘It is not annihilation
(numinous knowing is perfectly clear)
.’ The Patriarch said: ‘
This is the mind-substance transmitted by all the Buddhas; doubt it no more.
(Pointing at the Moon Record

[Numinous knowing] Numinous knowing is knowing without grasping at marks; to distinguish it from the mark-grasping knowing of seeing, hearing, sensing, and cognizing, it is called numinous knowing. The Shurangama Sutra says:
“To establish knowing upon seeing and knowing is the root of ignorance;
when seeing and knowing are without seeing, this is nirvāṇa, leak-free and truly pure
Master Hanshan’s Record of Contemplating the Laṅkāvatāra says:
“The mind is still and yet knows; true and false are both transcended—this is named the noble wisdom of self-awakening.”
Sengzhao’s Treatise on Prajñā Being Without Knowing says:

“Because the sage’s mind is without knowing, it is therefore all-knowing. The knowing of non-knowing is what is called omniscience. Hence the scripture says: ‘The sage’s mind knows nothing, yet knows everything.’ How true!”
Master Yongjia says:
“After
(having done away with)
conditions, there is utter stillness, and
the nature of numinous knowing
(the mind-substance)
is vividly clear
(perfectly distinct)
(Yongjia Anthology of the Chan School, “Hymn on Shamatha, Fourth”)
The method of practice is:
first, see one’s own original nature; then, guard and sustain it and remove habitual tendencies

(subduing affliction to break the heavy barrier, cutting off affliction to break the firm barrier, and even attaining the patient acceptance of the unborn and perfectly realizing the fruit of Buddhahood)

The Sixth Patriarch saw his own original nature when the Fifth Patriarch transmitted the Dharma to him at the third watch. Afterward, he concealed himself among the hunters for fifteen years—this was guarding and sustaining and removing habitual tendencies. Then, when the Way was accomplished, he came forth from the mountains. Therefore the Platform Sutra of the Sixth Patriarch teaches sudden awakening and gradual cultivation: seeing the nature, subduing affliction, cutting off affliction (cutting off the delusions of views and thoughts), attaining the patient acceptance of the unborn, and perfectly realizing the fruit of Buddhahood.
Old Man Yuanyin
A Brief Discussion of Understanding the Mind and Seeing the Nature
says:
“Now, having awakened to the Way
(seen one’s own original nature)

, one has clearly understood that one’s own empty and still numinous knowing is the true Buddha; but because the habitual defilements of many lives are deep, they cannot be wiped away at once, and when one meets with affairs one still gives rise to mind, and when one sees circumstances one still finds it hard to be without thought. Yet when mind arises and thoughts stir, one is not like the blind, who do not know that the dust of circumstances is fundamentally empty and so cling and grasp and wander on without returning. Instead, when the previous thought stirs, the next thought is aware of it and sweeps it away at once. One merely has traces of arising and ceasing, and a somewhat lesser strength, compared with one who is wholly unmoved in mind. But if one can guard and sustain it densely and continuously, ever aware and illumining, then as the days pass and the practice deepens, one will naturally become a single piece. The patriarchs of former generations herded the ox—this is the model for the work after awakening.” “Therefore one must, thought after thought, perfume and cultivate, mind after mind, be aware and illumine. After the great awakening, toward evil, cut off evil, yet cut off without cutting off
(without clinging to marks)

; toward good, cultivate good, yet cultivate without cultivating. Enter the hall and the inner chamber, return home and sit securely—this is what is called ‘the idle one of no-learning and non-doing.’”
Question:
Why is it said that the Platform Sutra of the Sixth Patriarch teaches sudden awakening and gradual cultivation?
Answer:
It has been said above that what Patriarch Bodhidharma transmitted was sudden awakening (
experientially realizing the mind-substance of no-thought
) and gradual cultivation. In the Platform Sutra of the Sixth Patriarch, in the section “Shenhui Pays His Respects” in “Chapter Eight: Sudden and Gradual,” it is recorded:
“The Master
(the Sixth Patriarch)
also said: If your mind is deluded and you do not see, ask a good teacher to seek the road; if your mind is awakened, then see the nature for yourself and cultivate according to the Dharma.”

(The Sixth Patriarch instructed Shenhui: if you have not yet seen the nature, you should ask a good teacher to point out the road so that you may see the nature; if you have already seen the nature, you should cultivate according to the Dharma.) From this it is clear that what the Sixth Patriarch transmitted was “first awakening (seeing the nature), then cultivating in dependence on the nature”—sudden awakening and gradual cultivation. The Chanyuan Yaolin Zhu records:
Formerly Lan’an visited Chan Master Baizhang, bowed, and asked: “If a student wishes to come to know the Buddha, which is it?” Baizhang said: “It is much like riding an ox while looking for an ox
(your self-nature is the Buddha; why speak of wishing to come to know the Buddha)
.” He asked: “After knowing, what then
(after knowing the Buddha (seeing the nature), what should one do)
?” Baizhang said: “It is like a person riding an ox home
(causing the self-nature to return to the source and restore the original)
.” He asked: “I do not yet understand how to guard and sustain it from beginning to end
(not knowing how, on the road home, one should guard and sustain it from first to last)
?” Baizhang said: “Like a cowherd holding his staff and watching it, not letting it trample people’s young crops
(cutting off habitual tendencies amid circumstances and conditions)
From this we know
that what the first patriarch of the Chan school, Bodhidharma, transmitted, what the Sixth Patriarch Huineng transmitted, and what

the Sixth Patriarch’s descendant Chan Master Baizhang (the Sixth Patriarch transmitted to Huairang, Huairang to Mazu, Mazu to Baizhang) transmitted, was in every case sudden awakening and gradual cultivation. Again, Baizhang transmitted to Weishan, and Weishan transmitted to Yangshan (the Weiyang school). The Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Huiji of Yangshan in Yuanzhou records:
“The Master
(Yangshan)

when he was a novice, a monk asked Shishuang: ‘What is the meaning of the Patriarch’s coming from the West?’ Shishuang said: ‘If a person in a well a thousand feet deep can get out without borrowing an inch of rope, that person will answer you the meaning of the coming from the West.’ The monk said: ‘Lately the monk Chang of Hunan has appeared in the world, and he too talks east and west for people.’ Shishuang called the novice: ‘Drag this corpse out.’ The Master later asked Danyuan: ‘How does the person in the well get out?’ Danyuan said: ‘Tut, foolish fellow! Who is in the well?’ The Master went and asked Weishan. Weishan called: ‘Huiji
(Yangshan’s name)

!’ The Master answered. Weishan said: ‘You are out!’ After the Master had settled, he often brought up these former words and said to the assembly: ‘I got my name at Danyuan’s place, and got my ground at Weishan’s place.’”
This shows that even down to what the Weiyang school transmitted, it was all sudden awakening and gradual cultivation.
Question: What the Sixth Patriarch transmitted is the sudden teaching; why is gradual cultivation spoken of here?

Answer: The sudden teaching means the teaching that “directly points to the source, passes through no stages, and sees the nature and becomes a Buddha.” In this teaching, becoming a Buddha passes through no stages, and so it is called “sudden.” Gradual cultivation refers to cultivating in dependence on the nature after seeing the nature, so as to perfect the Buddha Way. Therefore the “sudden” of the sudden teaching does not mean that after seeing the nature there is no need for further cultivation. In fact, in the Platform Sutra of the Sixth Patriarch a great part of the text is devoted to how to cultivate in dependence on the nature. As for the principle of sudden awakening and gradual cultivation, it is explained most clearly in the Juexin Jue; see in detail
A Detailed Explanation of the Juexin Jue

[Passing through no stages] Ordinarily a bodhisattva, cultivating from ordinary being to Buddhahood, must pass through fifty-two stages in all: the ten faiths, ten abidings, ten practices, ten dedications, ten grounds, equal enlightenment, and marvelous enlightenment. This takes three great asaṃkhyeya kalpas. The speed of practice in the Chan school, however, is vastly faster, and one does not pass through these stages one by one. [Seeing the nature and becoming a Buddha] Seeing one’s own original nature, then cultivating in dependence on the nature, and perfecting the Buddha Way. [Asaṃkhyeya kalpa] Rendered into Chinese as “innumerable kalpas.”
Question: Why sudden awakening and gradual cultivation? What is wrong with gradual cultivation first and sudden awakening afterward?

Answer: In fact, before sudden awakening there is also gradual cultivation, though it is usually called the preliminary practice before sudden awakening. When one already has the initial ability of not giving rise to a single thought, one should then see one’s own original nature. Afterward, cultivating in dependence on the nature is the correct path. If one sets seeing one’s own original nature aside and merely goes on cultivating gradually, the road is crooked and roundabout. The Platform Sutra of the Sixth Patriarch says: “Not knowing the original mind, learning the Dharma brings no benefit.” This is because, if one has not awakened to one’s own nature, one’s practice forever seeks within dharmas that arise and cease, and runs counter to the Way; hence the patriarchs rebuked it as “blind practice and foolish refinement.” This principle
is explained most clearly in the Juexin Jue; see in detail
A Detailed Explanation of the Juexin Jue
Question: What is “a single thought in accord”?

Answer: So-called “a single thought in accord” is suddenly according with the original nature. For example, listening to sutras and hearing the Dharma, studying and reading the scriptures and treatises, or hearing a pointing-out or inspiration concerning the nature of true suchness—at that moment according with the nature of true suchness, and experientially realizing the nature.
Question: What are kudzu vines?

Answer: Kudzu vines entangle a tree and cause it to wither. In the Chan gate, kudzu vines mean playing with words and language. Words and language were originally meant to expound Chan principles, point out the path, and seal and confirm states; yet they are often abused, leading people to manipulate karmic consciousness. Like kudzu vines spreading and interweaving, they instead leave the hearer bound and entangled. Investigating Chan is originally for the sake of ending birth and death, and even attaining the patient acceptance of the unborn and perfectly realizing the fruit of Buddhahood. Therefore all words and language that have nothing to do with how to make the ten thousand thoughts return to one, how to return the one to no-thing, how to see one’s own original nature, how to subdue affliction, how to cut off affliction, how to awaken to the unborn, and how to realize the fruit of Buddhahood are collectively called kudzu vines. Those harmed by them lightly waste their time, and gravely go astray. That Chan which clings to words and language and does not attain the true meaning is called literal Chan, or kudzu-vine Chan. It is what is meant by “sitting and talking, standing up and making meanings, mouth like a rushing torrent; when the moment comes and circumstances change, not one thing in a hundred can he do.” Master Hanshan says:
“Of old
(in former times)

the ancients left home for the sake of the great matter of birth and death. Even the Buddha and the patriarchs’ appearing in the world was solely to set forth this matter. There is no Buddhadharma apart from birth and death, and no birth and death apart from the Buddhadharma. It is as said: deluded about it, and birth and death begin; awakened to it, and saṃsāra ceases. Thus we know that the ancients who investigated and sought took their stand only at the crossroads of birth and death, seeking what is certain and ultimate; they did not, apart from this, take paper, ink, and written words, or the three vehicles and twelve divisions of the teachings, as some marvelous special thing.”
(Mengyou ji, · “Instruction to the Seat-Master Miaozhan”)
Question: What is wild-fox Chan?

Answer: Studying the Way yet drifting into deviant and crooked views, seeming right but not being right, and claiming awakening without having awakened—the Chan school denounces all of this as “wild-fox Chan.” The phrase comes from the public case “Baizhang and the Wild Fox”: There was an old man who often listened to the Dharma where Chan Master Baizhang was; when the assembly withdrew, the old man withdrew too. One day he did not withdraw, and the Master asked: ‘Who is the one standing before me?’ The old man said: ‘Yes! I am not a man. In the time of Kāśyapa Buddha in the past I once dwelt on this mountain. Because a student asked me: Does a greatly cultivated person still fall under cause and effect? I answered: He does not fall under cause and effect. For five hundred lives I fell into the body of a wild fox. Now I beg the Master to turn a phrase in my place, so that I may be freed from the wild fox.’ So he asked: ‘Does a greatly cultivated person still fall under cause and effect?’ The Master said: ‘He is not blind to cause and effect.’ At these words the old man had a great awakening. He said: Now I am already freed from the wild fox body; tomorrow, behind the mountain, I beg that my body be cremated according to the rites for a deceased monk. (For annotations see in detail
Baizhang and the Wild Fox
Question: Nowadays heretical teachings and non-Buddhist paths swarm like bees; how should one tell them apart?

Answer: The Buddhadharma is for the sake of ending birth and death (both fragmentary birth and death and transformational birth and death), and only what can end birth and death is Buddhadharma. Body, mind, and world—there is no marvel that does not exist; many so-called paranormal phenomena and wondrous states are nothing but deluded attributions and deluded designations upon an illusory body and mind, and none of them has any ground (none of them can end birth and death). Therefore a student of Buddhism should use this (whether or not it can end birth and death) to tell them apart, and must not go astray and take the road of no return.
[The Buddhadharma is for the sake of ending birth and death, and only what can end birth and death is Buddhadharma] Master Hanshan says:
“Of old
(in former times)

the ancients left home for the sake of the great matter of birth and death. Even the Buddha and the patriarchs’ appearing in the world was solely to set forth this matter. There is no Buddhadharma apart from birth and death, and no birth and death apart from the Buddhadharma. It is as said: deluded about it, and birth and death begin; awakened to it, and saṃsāra ceases. Thus we know that the ancients who investigated and sought took their stand only at the crossroads of birth and death, seeking what is certain and ultimate; they did not, apart from this, take paper, ink, and written words, or the three vehicles and twelve divisions of the teachings, as some marvelous special thing.”
(Mengyou ji, · “Instruction to the Seat-Master Miaozhan”)

One who has seen the nature should break through the delusion of views. Here we excerpt a passage discussing birth and death from True Mind Directly Explained, “The True Mind Leaves Birth and Death” (for annotations see in detail
A Discussion of Birth and Death
). It is hoped that readers will deeply realize and enter into “no birth and death,” and then apply no birth and death amid circumstances and conditions

[Delusion of views] The delusion of views is the ordinary person’s confusion and error in views, such as the five wrong views: the view of the body (the wrong view that deludedly clings to the body as truly existing), the extreme view, the wrong view, the view of grasping views, and the view of grasping at precepts and prohibitions.

“Someone says: I have heard that one who has seen the nature escapes birth and death. Yet the patriarchs of old were men who had seen the nature, and they all had birth and had death; and now we plainly see that people who cultivate the Way in the world have the matter of birth and death. How can it be said that they escape birth and death?
“The reply: Birth and death are fundamentally non-existent; they are falsely reckoned to exist. It is like a person with diseased eyes who sees flowers in empty space
(flowers)
. Or a person without disease says
(or one without eye disease says)
: There are no flowers in empty space. The sick person
(the one with diseased eyes)

does not believe it. If the eye disease is cured, the flowers in empty space vanish of themselves, and only then does he believe that the flowers do not exist. Yet even before the flowers vanish, the flowers are also empty; it is only that the sick person deludedly clings to them as flowers, and they do not truly exist as a substance. Likewise a person deludedly takes birth and death to exist; or one without birth and death tells him: There is fundamentally no birth and death. One day, when his delusion ceases, birth and death vanish of themselves, and only then does he know that birth and death were fundamentally non-existent. Even when birth and death have not ceased, they are not truly existent either, because he deludedly takes birth and death to exist.
The sutra
(the Sutra of Perfect Enlightenment)

says: ‘Good sons, all living beings, from beginningless time, have all manner of inverted views, like a confused person who takes the four directions to be changed about; they deludedly take the four great elements as the mark of their own body, and the shadowy reflections of the six dusts as the mark of their own mind, just as a person with diseased eyes sees flowers in empty space. And so it is even to the point that when the many flowers in empty space vanish into empty space, one cannot say there is a fixed place where they vanish. Why? Because there is no place where they were born. All living beings, within the unborn, deludedly see arising and ceasing; therefore it is called turning about in birth and death.’

From this passage of scripture we know with confidence that one who thoroughly awakens to the perfect-enlightenment true mind is fundamentally without birth and death. That we now know there is no birth and death, and yet cannot escape birth and death, is because our practice has not yet reached the mark. Hence it is said in the teachings that the woman Ambapālī asked Mañjuśrī: ‘Clearly knowing that birth is the dharma of non-arising, why is one swept along by birth and death?’ Mañjuśrī said: ‘Because his power is not yet full.’ Later there was Jin, a mountain master, who asked Xiu, a mountain master: ‘Clearly knowing that birth is the dharma of non-arising, why is one still swept along by birth and death?’ Xiu said: ‘A bamboo shoot will after all become bamboo; can it be used as a bamboo strip right now?’

Therefore, to know no birth and death is not as good as to embody no birth and death; to embody no birth and death is not as good as to accord with no birth and death; to accord with no birth and death is not as good as to use no birth and death. People today do not even know no birth and death, let alone embody it, accord with it, or use it! Hence those who take birth and death as real do not believe in the dharma of no birth and death—is that not only fitting!”

After seeing the nature (breaking the initial barrier), one must do the work of guarding and sustaining. The work of guarding is subduing affliction (breaking the heavy barrier), while the work of letting be is cutting off affliction (penetrating the firm barrier). Afflictions are thousand upon thousand and ten thousand upon ten thousand, but summed up they are the three poisons: greed, anger, and delusion.

[The three poisons] Poison means harm. Greed, anger, and delusion harm the supramundane wholesome mind, and so are named poisons. 1. The poison of greed: the mind of drawing in and taking is called greed. If with a deluded mind one draws in and takes toward all pleasing circumstances, this is named the poison of greed. 2. The poison of anger: the mind of wrath is called anger. If with a deluded mind one gives rise to wrath toward all displeasing circumstances, this is named the poison of anger. 3. The poison of delusion: the mind of confusion is called delusion. If toward all matters and principles one is without understanding, and inverted and deluded one grasps and gives rise to wrong actions, this is named the poison of delusion.

Among the three poisons of greed, anger, and delusion, greed is the root, and both anger and delusion arise from greed. Because one cannot obtain what one craves, or loses what one craves, anger arises; because one craves, one goes against principle, and delusion arises. Therefore, to extinguish affliction, one must put effort into cutting off craving.
